title: Fallout Shelters: Probably Useless (Let’s Never Find Out)
summary: Josh and Chuck open with audiobook news (recording the Stuff You Should Know audiobook, preorder gifts, not new episodes) and a squirrel attack anecdote. The main topic is Cold War fallout shelters: why they were considered, the nuclear arms race and civil-defense thinking, types of radiation (alpha, beta, gamma, neutrons) and fallout, protection factor (PF) ratings, the Gaither Report, Kennedy's 1961 National Fallout Shelter Survey and its cost, the fallout shelter sign and its 3M production, Meals for Millions food and Bulgur wheat biscuits, other countries' shelter programs (USSR, Sweden, Switzerland, UK, Australia), the Oak Ridge National Laboratory family-built shelter pamphlet, and the program's shutdown and sign removal. The episode ends with a listener mail correction about Australian Aboriginal terminology and an apology for ads run in Australia.
topics: Oak Ridge National Laboratory fallout shelter pamphlet

segments.title: Opening banter and audiobook news
segments.summary: The hosts discuss recording their Stuff You Should Know audiobook, that it is not new podcast episodes, preorder gifts, and a squirrel attack anecdote, then set up the fallout shelter topic.

segments.title: Cold War fallout shelters and the nuclear threat
segments.summary: Introduction to fallout shelters as a reflection of Cold War anxiety during the nuclear arms race. Kennedy's request for public shelter funding, Chuck's father's shelter project, and the early government stance that people should build their own shelters.

segments.title: Blast effects and types of radiation
segments.summary: Discussion of blast radius of a megaton bomb, the B-83 bomb, and the different radiation types: alpha, beta, gamma, and neutrons, along with how fallout spreads and contaminates food and water.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with a brief reference to the audiobook and preorders.

segments.title: Protection factor and shelter types
segments.summary: Explanation of the protection factor (PF) rating from FEMA standards, with a minimum of forty suggested and about three hundred preferred. Discussion of public versus private shelters and the Meals for Millions food and bulgur wheat crackers stocked in shelters.

segments.title: Private shelter craze and Gaither Report
segments.summary: The 1957 Gaither Report and its conclusion that prevention was key, the resulting private shelter trend, Milwaukee and Woodland Hills shelters, and the Family Room of Tomorrow.

segments.title: Kennedy survey, national program, and international shelters
segments.summary: Kennedy's 1961 letter in Life magazine announcing the National Fallout Shelter Survey, its cost of roughly 190 million dollars, and how the USSR, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK, and Australia approached shelters. The government then marked buildings with the fallout shelter sign made by 3M.

segments.title: Shelter limitations, Oak Ridge pamphlet, and program shutdown
segments.summary: Criticism of the public program as poorly stocked and ill-conceived, Robert Clara's article, the Oyster-Adams school shelter, the recommended two-week stay, and the Oak Ridge pamphlet with a family-built shelter achieving a PF around 300. The program ended in the 1970s and the last signs were removed in New York City in 2017.

segments.title: Listener mail: Aboriginal terminology correction
segments.summary: A listener (Tanita) corrects the hosts' use of the term Aborigines in the Wetlands episode, noting outdated terminology and the need to name specific peoples; the hosts also address ads run in Australia.
